newsitem.title: USA: France clashes with U.S. on Romania NATO membership.
newsitem.headline: France clashes with U.S. on Romania NATO membership.

text.p: France attacked the United States on Friday for refusing to change its stance against giving Romania early membership of the NATO military alliance.

A spokeswoman for French President Jacques Chirac said he had raised the question in talks with President Bill Clinton but made no headway in finding a compromise ahead of a NATO summit in Madrid next month.
"We would like this problem to be solved. We would do it more easily if the American position were different," Chirac spokeswoman Catherine Colonna told a news conference.
Chirac told reporters earlier it would be in the interests of Europe and Romania for it to be in the first group of countries joining NATO.
Leaders of the world's rich nations in the Group of Seven were in Denver for their annual summit.

A U.S. official said Washington did not think Romania was ready to join the pact. The United States has said that only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic should be in the first wave of new NATO members.
U.S. National Security Adviser Sandy Berger told reporters after the one-hour Clinton-Chirac meeting that Clinton had not changed his views on the subject.

"He does not believe that this is the time to go forward with Romania," Berger said, adding that Clinton favoured an "aggressive open-door policy" for nations to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation in the future.
"I'm sure that President Clinton didn't change his mind, but I think they listened to each other," Berger said.
The United States surprised its allies last week by saying its firm position was that only three former Warsaw Pact states should join the pact in the first wave.

Colonna said France would continue to press for a solution on Romania. She said one compromise would be for negotiations on Romanian membership to start at the same time as the others. The talks would then go on at different paces depending on the country involved.
"We will try to find a compromise before Madrid, but it is not easy given the American position reaffirmed by President Clinton today," Colonna said.
Germany said it had not decided whether to press for Romania and Slovenia to join Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic in entering NATO.
"We have not yet set the position of the federal government," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said. "For us three, four or five (new members) would be thinkable."

NATO leaders meet in Madrid July 8-9 to invite the countries selected to begin membership negotiations. The United States has set 1999, the alliance's 50th anniversary, as the target date for their admission.
